children.text:
That was my thought as well, that what we're really talking about here is an inversion of our current values, or more accurately the first time that our assumptions about them can be challenged and tested in an automated fashion.

As in: does competition or cooperation produce greater economic gains in terms of cost of living, quality of life, etc?

Subjectively, I've been forced to live and work under a competitive capitalist system that goes against most of my instincts for my entire adult life, which has resulted in a profoundly negative economic outcome for myself.

Others I know have done better, either finding ways to tread water as independent freelancers/artisans or managing to save modest nest eggs (although only by finding themselves on the winning side of the stock market, rarely/never through work at a job).

Vanishingly few have reached economic independence by winning the internet lottery for example, and I don't know them personally.

So based on the evidence before me, competition is a failed model. Yes yes, I'm writing this on an electronic device that cost billions of dollars of R&D to produce. I have food in my stomach and a roof over my head. But have I worked on important problems that would advance the state of the art in my chosen field? Of course not. And neither have most of you reading this.

So I would rephrase the question: will AI allow us to explore cooperation as an alternative economic model to the one we have?

I believe that it will, but not from the top down. If we wait for the wealthy and powerful to share, we'll be waiting forever. No, progress now must come from the most downtrodden among us creating alternative ways to provide time/money/resources to the underemployed and indigent so that they can finally self-actualize outside of the status quo.

Specifically, that means automating necessity. How do I acquire enough money to pay for my food and shelter today, even if I don't have a job? How can I acquire enough money to provide for myself, someone else, and some children (my personal definition of success) without being beholden to an employer? How can I remain insulated from inflation and the tendency for the owners of private property (not personal property) to devalue currency to make the means of production they own more profitable? How can I pay this forward to the next generation so that they can become educated and someday enjoy the commons which I myself have enjoyed? And so on and so forth.

If AI can't do those things, then frankly change may remain forever out of reach. Which makes the question of whether specific fields like math and science will benefit rather moot.

children.text:
I respect and have had good experiences with mathematicians.

My take on how fields evolve is informed by the history of mathematics, computing, art, and music.

Current times offer both a sense of loss and a call to opportunity. I have heard more about the sense of loss, so I hope to draw interest more towards the opportunity.

The past few months have, among other things, illustrated to me how many people feel hurt by past experiences with mathematicians, and how this, not always unreasonably, colors their opinions of the field and its future today.

Obviously a golden age.

I’m not bitter about this anymore — it’s been a long time. But the story holds something.

Back in the day, I knew I was talented at mathematics, and I wanted to pursue a research career. For a freshman research class, I selected a problem that was intentionally outside my comfort zone, and came up with some cool ideas. It wasn’t publication quality, though the course wasn’t really expecting publications.

Framing the problem in a way that it could be solved with calculus turned out to be a key insight. I turned to Wolfram, since the integrals were beyond what I as a freshman could have done myself, and I understood that the insight that produced the solution was my original work. I don’t think anyone in the class could have done those integrals. The instructor himself couldn’t tell me what was wrong with them if anything. Yet, he was unimpressed and subtly dismissive or critical.

Today, I might have been in the wave of researchers developing AI for mathematics work. The instructor could have been proud of shaping mathematics through his mentorship. The university might have invited me for talks. Instead, I ended up leaving mathematics as a field altogether. Now, I write software for a bank.

The world is as rich as we make it. Don’t let your opportunities and potential expire. Embrace the materials that are available to work with, or someone else will and they will out compete you and you will have missed the moment.

I get that there’s a romantic idea of what mathematicians do, and the field changing creates a sort of identity crisis. I would argue that the field has entered a new era. Exploring and shaping this era of mathematics is the opportunity of a lifetime. Embrace it, drive it, and make your mark.

children.text:
Yes, you're right, understanding informs the constraints and the possible solution spaces. That should be added to the list.

Practically speaking, I don't think the "black box" metaphor is as broken as you're saying, though I like the point you made. There is still a ton of software (the majority, I think -- crud apps of all flavors) where an unthinking, untechnical PM wants something they can specify, and an LLM can give it to them, and it will more or less solve their problem. It won't be the best possible thing, but it will be good enough.

This:

> In the pre-LLM era, the economic value of "understanding" and "shared knowledge" about the programs themselves was only that it made maintenance and changes cheaper.

This only holds if there is a bright line separation between the problem, the solution, and the implementation of the solution. And that is not the case.

Understanding the implementation frequently improves your understanding of the solution, which improves your understanding of the problem, which leads to better solutions. Sometimes it leads to realizing that there is a completely different problem you should be solving.

So what I’m refuting is that there is no value to understanding the program.

But beyond that black box products that users know how to use but don’t understand is also a vast oversimplification.

Frequently software is useful specifically because it forces users to adopt a process not just because it allows them to do something they were previously doing faster. In those cases the process is usually informed by the implementation, so the user needs to understand parts of the implementation even if it’s indirectly.

I don't disagree with the points you've made but what are they rebutting?

The economic value is still the product you delivered. Your understanding of the implementation meant you participated in the work of the "product manager". I think most good devs do. That might be an argument for devs to transition into designer/PM roles. That is effectively happening already, whether or not role titles have caught up.

But in any case the value isn't in the understanding itself. It just happens that the understanding still helps create better block box products. Also, I wouldn't count on this "human advantage" lasting long. I hope it does, but ime LLMs are now good enough to do this "co-design" too, and will only get better.

Only if you assume that all software works the way that product managers think it does.

They come up with the features and the implementation is an unimportant detail in realizing their designs.

In reality implementation details frequently drive design and in most cases they are at least highly intertwined.

I can’t count how many products and features I’ve built that ended working completely differently than the initial design, or how many times I was able to simplify a workflow after spending a days thinking about the implementation details.

You can kinda do something similar by spending days or weeks going back and forth with an LLM, but at least in my experience that doesn’t really save much time and I don’t understand the problem quite as well by the end of it.

The parallel is real, but in math the "cash value" of the results often won't appear for years, if at all, and so the teaching and "intellectual fortification" is the primary point of the whole enterprise (at least, a major part of it).

In contrast, the value of a program is typically just the "black box" service it provides. Indeed, the program itself has always been opaque to most business stakeholders. Before, they paid human programmers and got back a program they didn't understand but could use; now, they pay an LLM provider and get back a program they don't understand but can use. In the pre-LLM era, the economic value of "understanding" and "shared knowledge" about the programs themselves was only that it made maintenance and changes cheaper. It never had intrinsic value, except as intellectual satisfaction to programmers (I was... am... one of those who found that value).

children.author: dualvariable
children.text:
I think I'm a bit on the "golden age" side of the question.

The math slopocalypse isn't useful without being able to turn it into math that can be taught to actual humans by finding the underlying unifying principles.

All those O(n log(n)^(1-delta)) results suggest that there's probably a unifying "trick" behind all of them and that there's going to be an upper bound on delta for any problem. You should really be able to teach that in a textbook and then have any human student replicate any of the LLM results as worked problems.

For anything that an LLM manages to prove with thousands or millions of lines of Lean code, there's likely a missing branch of mathematics sitting there somewhere.

Actual humans need to beat on the problems and the LLM-generated solutions until they come up with the underlying principles, probably using AI to help them do it.

You probably won't get there by just asking an LLM to invent a new branch of mathematics and "don't make any mistakes"; the mathematicians who get good at directing LLMs to search for unifying principles, and then synthesizing (and double-checking) the results, will likely be very successful in their field.

> For those hard theorems where we really want LLMs to help us, these Lean proofs are extremely long, like hundreds of thousands of lines of code long. A seemingly emergent trend is that the longer the Lean version of a proof, the messier and less faithful its machine-generated “natural language” translation seems to be.

This seems to be a common and continuing objection to the OpenAI math repo release. Specifically that at least some, perhaps many of

  * the natural language proofs are low quality or otherwise extremely difficult to understand (although possibly correct?)
  * the lean proofs are too long, convoluted, or otherwise extremely difficult to understand
I wonder if LLMs will be able to generate "high quality" natural language and lean proofs soon.

And specifically: iterate on the OpenAI repo to produce "better" proofs that prove the same things.

children.author: Balgair
children.text:
Terry remarks in a Nymberphile video that he thinks the Heroic age of mathematics is now over. the age of individual researchers is done, and hhatnlike many other disciplines, mathematics will be done in large teams, big facilities, and in complex ways that no sole individual will understand end to end.

I imagine he means in that video something like modern physics at CERN where no one single person actually understand how the whole thing works, but nonetheless is confident in the results.

I find Terry's hypothesis there somewhat comforting to my own limited cranium. most of the math he does already is far beyond me, nevertheless I trust that he is correct.

it's a different world for math, but one we all readily inhabit already everything we cross a bridge or buy refrigerated food.
